projects.name: 3.2.5 Data Insights for Social and Humanitarian Action (Phase 2)
projects.description:
Global Data Access Initiative (GDAI) is an initiative managed by UNOPS and the Executive Office of the Secretary General (EOSG) across UN Global Pulse (UNGP) in collaboration with UN agencies (World Food Program (WFP), the UN Development Program (UNDP), private sector partners, and foundations. GDAI aspires to catalyst the formation of a connected and cohesive ecosystem of “plug-and-play” data and AI products and services including the responsible access to, use, and reuse of data thereby accelerating the attainment of the SDGs. 

GDAI will build and deploy two scalable, productionized solutions to problems faced by frontline organizations focusing on natural disaster response and recovery in close collaboration with, and informed by the needs of WFP and UNDP: Vulnerability mapping and population assessment and; Disaster damage assessment. In building these solutions, the team will take an approach that aims at scalable products for these use cases and beyond. This will result in a collection of “plug-and-play” data and AI products and services that can be used to accelerate the delivery of solutions in pursuit of the SDGs whilst generating insights into how to best evolve and, over time, realise the vision of GDAI beyond natural disaster response and recovery.

UNOPS is tasked for the provision of operational services to the UN Global Pulse to operationalize SDG specific use cases leveraging data from private sector and other entities across countries in Asia. 

In 2023, GDAI was renamed DISHA (Data Insights for Social and Humanitarian Action) to better reflect the goal of the initiative and to show what the personnel wants to achieve with the data. projects.name: 1.1.7 Implementation an acceleration programme on family planning in districts with low modern contraceptive prevalence rates
projects.description: Sub-output measures the number of administrative districts within Indonesia that: have been identified as having a low modern Contraceptive Prevalence Rate (mCPR) based on a defined threshold (below national benchmark) and are actively implementing an acceleration program specifically designed to improve family planning (FP) access and uptake. Modern Contraceptive Prevalence Rate (mCPR): mCPR refers to the percentage of women of reproductive age (typically 15-49) who are currently using a modern method of contraception. Modern methods typically include (but are not limited to) oral contraceptive pills, injectables, implants, intrauterine devices (IUDs), condoms, and sterilization. The specific definition of "modern methods" used should be consistent with national definitions and clearly documented. Low mCPR: This signifies that the district's mCPR is below national benchmark, indicating a need for targeted interventions to improve access to and uptake of modern contraception.  Acceleration Programme: This refers to a focused and intensified set of activities designed to rapidly increase mCPR in the targeted districts. This focus set of activities are tailored based on evidence and data of the district.  Family Planning: This emphasizes that family planning services are provided in a way that respects, protects, and fulfills the reproductive rights of individuals. This includes ensuring informed choice, voluntary participation, accessibility, availability, acceptability, and quality of services. Selection of targeted districts: the targeted districts are those having mCPR below national benchmark as stipulated in Head of BKKBN Decree No. 141/KEP/E3/2024 Year 2024 concerning Priority Location for Family Planning and Reproductive Health and MOH regulation No. 2 Year 2025 on implementation of reproductive health efforts. projects.name: 1.1.2 Accreditation of government and private midwifery schools as per national pre-service midwifery education standards that are aligned with the International Confederation of Midwives (ICM) standards.
projects.description:
The International Confederation of Midwives developed the Global Standards in Midwifery Education in response to calls to standardise and improve midwifery education and training across the world. The ICM has a clear definition of midwife to support both education and regulation standardisation. 
The Global Standards for Midwifery Education provide a benchmark for programmes leading to registration/ recognition as a midwife. This indicator counts the cumulative total of government and private midwifery schools that comply with national pre-service midwifery education standards.
 There are six ICM Standards that provide a benchmark for midwifery education and training programmes: ● Organisation and Administration ● Midwifery Faculty ● Student Body ● Curriculum ● Resources, Facilities and Services ● Assessment Strategies/Quality Improvement The Standards were developed using a recognised consensus research methodology (Modified Delphi Process) with midwifery education experts from across low, middle and high-income countries. They are the minimum standards expected of a midwifery programme. A crucial element of the implementation of the standards is through deep approaches to learning. Deep approaches to learning relies on learners having the time to integrate new knowledge and to apply this new knowledge in supported practice settings. If graduates are expected to be able to practice in a way that meets the essential competencies of the midwife then they require time to gain the necessary skills, knowledge and behaviours.  Midwifery schools in this context refer to midwifery study programs, both Diploma 3 (D3) and professional programs, with priority given to professional programs, in both public and private universities.

projects.name: 3.2.6 UN Global Pulse Asia Pacific (Phase 2)
projects.description:
UN Global Pulse serves as the United Nations Secretary-General's flagship innovation initiative, established in 2009 to harness the power of big data and technology for sustainable development. Functioning as the UN's innovation laboratory, Global Pulse operates at the intersection of data science, technology, and development to generate insights that inform evidence-based policy-making. The initiative originated in response to the recognition that traditional methods of data collection and analysis were insufficient to address the rapidly evolving challenges faced by the international community.

The core mandate of UN Global Pulse revolves around leveraging emerging technologies, including artificial intelligence and big data analytics, to unlock real-time, actionable insights. By doing so, Global Pulse aims to enhance the UN system's ability to respond effectively to global crises, accelerate progress towards the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), and address complex socio-economic challenges. Over the years, UN Global Pulse has pioneered innovative approaches to data analysis, experimentation, and collaboration. The initiative has actively engaged with governments, the private sector, academia, and civil society to build a network of Pulse Labs worldwide. These labs serve as localized hubs, exploring how data innovation can contribute to more effective and targeted development interventions at the country level.

The initiative to transition Pulse Lab Jakarta (PLJ) into the UN Global Pulse Asia-Pacific Hub marks a pivotal phase for the UN Global Pulse in the Asia Pacific region. Shifting from country-level activities, the Regional Hub will now assume a broader regional role, focusing on convening stakeholders, sharing information, knowledge management, advocacy, and standard-setting. UN Global Pulse Asia-Pacific aims to enhance efficiency in digital innovation efforts, contribute to policy-making, and address issues of exclusion and bias. 

The project is activated through a grant from the UN Foundation and aims at leveraging big data and artificial intelligence to achieve Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) in the Asia-Pacific region. The expanded scope includes emphasizing successful scaling, scanning regional gaps and challenges, and fostering broader innovation capabilities. The project design aligns with UN Global Pulse Core Functions, encompassing digital innovation programs, strategic foresight, and support for inclusive digital innovation policies. 

The project's theory of change outlines three impact channels: Innovation Solutions, Innovation Services & Capability Building, and Advocacy & Thought Leadership. These channels collectively aim to accelerate delivery, induce policy transformations, and generate social impact across the Asia-Pacific region. The project's programmatic considerations include stakeholder and communication management, partnership engagement, sustainable results management, gender mainstreaming, capacity building, and risk management.

The governance mechanism involves a Regional Steering Committee comprising the Government of Indonesia, multilateral, and philanthropic donors, responsible for providing strategic direction, advocacy, and overseeing program performance. The project team structure is designed for flexibility and efficiency, leveraging UNOPS support services and recruiting specialists to deliver on program objectives. 

UNOPS and UNGP-AP

The UNOPS team managing the UNGP-AP project brings its extensive expertise in project management, procurement, and operational support to ensure the successful establishment and functioning of the Regional Hub. UNOPS, known for its commitment to excellence in project delivery and adherence to the highest standards of transparency, efficiency, and accountability, will have to play a crucial role in overseeing the day-to-day operations of the Asia-Pacific initiative.

UNOPS will provide comprehensive support in the areas of fund management, administration, human resource management, procurement, and legal arrangements for strategic partnerships, including data partnerships and technical collaborations. Leveraging its vast experience in managing complex, multi-stakeholder projects, UNOPS will have to facilitate the smooth transition of Pulse Lab Jakarta into the UN Global Pulse Asia-Pacific Hub.

In addition to operational support, UNOPS will contribute to risk management, ensuring that the project adheres to UNOPS risk management strategy and engages in continuous evaluation and mitigation of potential challenges. The organization's commitment to sustainability will be integral to the project's success, with a focus on mainstreaming gender considerations, promoting diversity, and addressing climate impacts throughout the implementation.

projects.name: 1.1.14 Implementation of newly developed and institutionalized reproductive health education in the national curriculum
projects.description: This indicator tracks the progress of integrating comprehensive reproductive health (RH) education into the school national curriculum system, thereby  empowering school-aged children and youth with the knowledge and skills necessary for reproductive health and contributing to the prevention of VAWG and harmful practices. Institutionalization in the national curriculum refers to the integration of the RH education  into intra-curricular, intracurricular, co-curricular, or extracurricular according to the Indonesian regulation on the national curriculum structure.  The reproductive health curriculum will be developed based on two primary references: first, the reproductive health education module—approved by the Ministry of Primary and Secondary Education and the Ministry of Health, and set to be adapted according to Indonesian social and cultural norms and children and youth aged 7-18 year development—and second, the current curriculum assessment led by UNFPA, UGM, the Ministry of Education, and the Ministry of Health, which will serve as the foundation for the new curriculum's implementation. This indicator measures the number of schools (both government and private, including those managed by non-governmental and faith-based organizations) that have officially adopted and demonstrably implemented the newly developed and institutionalized RH education curriculum. Schools implement RH education curriculum when  1)  the RH education content must be demonstrably integrated into the school’s regular educational activities. This integration can take various forms, including incorporation into existing subject curricula, dedicated counseling sessions, character education programs, or locally tailored subjects designed to address specific community needs;  2)  the teachers responsible for delivering this RH education must have successfully completed the training for teachers’ programme approved by the Ministry of Primary and Secondary Education. This ensures that educators are equipped with the necessary knowledge, skills, and pedagogical approaches to effectively impart RH education in a manner consistent with national standards and best practices.

projects.name: 3.2.1 Assessment of Digital Governance and Digital Rights During the 2025 Crisis
projects.description: UNESCO, through its Social Media 4 Peace initiative, worked with ELSAM and the Damai Coalition to assess how digital governance during the August–September 2025 crisis affected digital rights in Indonesia, particularly freedom of expression and access to information. The project involves collecting and analyzing data on actions taken by the government, digital platforms, and civil society, and identifying issues such as internet disruptions, content moderation, and digital threats. Based on the findings, the Contractor will prepare an analytical report with recommendations, develop advocacy and communication materials, and support the Coalition’s efforts to promote transparent, rights‑respecting digital governance. The activity started on December 2025.

projects.name: 3.2.2 Strengthening Digital Governance and Policy Reform Through Evidence‑Based Research and Advocacy
projects.description: UNESCO, through the Social Media 4 Peace initiative, is partnering with ECPAT Indonesia to support the Damai Coalition in advancing inclusive and accountable digital governance in Indonesia by conducting comprehensive research, multi‑stakeholder consultations, and targeted advocacy. The contractor will map Indonesia’s digital regulatory landscape, validate findings, develop a 2030 policy reform roadmap, and prepare a two‑year Coalition advocacy workplan; produce a policy paper on derivative regulations of the Internet and Electronic Transactions Law (Articles 40 and 40A); and lead a major study on children’s age‑restriction regulations for social media and online games through surveys, interviews, expert discussions, public consultations, and dissemination meetings. Responsibilities include organizing workshops, focus groups, consultations, and stakeholder meetings; producing reports, audiovisual materials, and communication outputs; maintaining regular coordination with UNESCO; ensuring gender-sensitive implementation; and adhering to visibility, transparency, and intellectual property requirements.
